meaning: Expresses the speaker's own desire to do something (first-person wish): "I want to ...". In questions, it asks about the listener's wishes.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + たい (e.g. 行きます→行きたい, 食べます→食べたい, します→したい)
usage: 「〜たい」 itself conjugates like an i-adjective: たい／たくない／たかった／たくなかった／たくて／たければ. For polite speech add 「です」: 行きたいです, 行きたくないです.
In principle it only expresses the wishes of the speaker (first person), or of the listener (second person) in questions. For a third person, use 「〜たがる／たがっている」, or 「〜たいと言っている」, 「〜たいそうだ」, etc.
The object can be marked with 「を」, but 「が」 is also common to highlight the thing desired: 水を飲みたい／水が飲みたい. Particles of other verbs such as 「〜に会う」 or 「〜へ行く」 stay unchanged.
Asking a superior or an elder directly with 「〜たいですか」 sounds presumptuous; use softer forms such as 「〜なさいますか」 or 「〜はいかがですか」 instead.
「〜たい」 is very common after 「〜てみる」 and 「〜ている」: 食べてみたい (I'd like to try eating it), ずっとここにいたい (I want to stay here forever).
scenarios: Talking about your own wishes in everyday conversation: 「夏休みに北海道へ行きたいです。」
Asking a friend what they want: 「何が食べたい？」
The negative expresses not feeling like doing something: 「今日はどこにも出かけたくない。」
The past tense recalls a past wish or expresses regret: 「子どものころ、パイロットになりたかった。」
Stating aspirations in applications or essays: 「将来は日本の会社で働きたいと考えています。」
etymology: Modern 「たい」 comes from the Classical Japanese desiderative auxiliary 「たし」 (conjugated like a ku-type adjective). Its attributive form 「たき」 became 「たい」 through i-onbin (sound change to い) and replaced the conclusive form as the modern form. 「たし」 began to appear in the late Heian period, and from the Kamakura period onward it gradually replaced 「まほし」, the Heian-period auxiliary of desire. As for the origin of 「たし」, one theory links it to the adjective 「いたし」 (甚し, "extreme, intense"), but this is not settled. Because it developed from an adjective-type auxiliary, modern 「たい」 still conjugates like an i-adjective.
examples: I want to go to Hokkaido during summer vacation.
I want to drink some cold water.
I don't want to go anywhere today.
When I was a child, I wanted to become a pilot.
I've been thinking I'd like to try authentic ramen at least once.

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: 「ほしい」 means wanting a thing and follows a noun; 「〜たい」 means wanting to do an action and follows a verb. Wanting a car: 車がほしい; wanting to buy a car: 車を買いたい.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 「〜たい」 is only a wish and may never be carried out; 「つもり」 means you already intend or plan to do it. 行きたい (I want to go) ≠ 行くつもりだ (I plan to go).

similar.title: 〜たがる
similar.explanation: Used for a third person's wishes: 弟はゲームを買いたがっている (My little brother wants to buy a game). Use 「〜たい」 for yourself and 「〜たがる」 for others.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: 「行こうと思う」 expresses the speaker's present decision or intention; it is closer to actually doing it than 「行きたい」 and sounds more certain.

meaning: Please (do something). Used to politely request, instruct, or urge the listener to do an action.
connection: Verb te-form + ください (e.g. 待つ→待ってください, 読む→読んでください, 見る→見てください)
usage: 「ください」 is the imperative form of the honorific verb 「くださる」, so 「〜てください」 is essentially a polite command or request; the listener has little room to refuse.
Watch the voicing in the te-form: godan verbs ending in む・ぶ・ぬ・ぐ become 「〜んで／〜いで」: 読んでください, 泳いでください.
For more politeness use a question form: 「〜てくださいませんか」, 「〜ていただけませんか」; among friends say 「〜て」, 「〜てね」, or 「〜てくれる？」.
For a negative request (please don't), use 「〜ないでください」; 「〜てくださらない」 is not used this way.
It can also be written with kanji as 「〜て下さい」, but modern official documents and newspapers tend to write 「ください」 in kana.
scenarios: A teacher giving instructions to students: 「教科書の30ページを開いてください。」
Service settings such as shop staff or station announcements: 「白線の内側までお下がりください。」 (the honorific pattern 「お〜ください」)
Asking a stranger for help: 「すみません、ちょっと待ってください。」
Advice or precautions from doctors, instruction leaflets, etc.: 「この薬は食後に飲んでください。」
Urging or warmly inviting someone: 「どうぞ、たくさん食べてください。」
etymology: 「ください」 is the imperative of the verb 「くださる」 (下さる). 「くださる」 comes from 「くだす」 (下す, originally "to hand down from above, to bestow") plus the honorific auxiliary 「る」, meaning "a superior bestows something on an inferior". Its imperative was originally 「くだされ」, which changed to 「ください」 from the Edo period onward. Literally, 「〜てください」 means "please bestow on me the favor of (doing this action)", which gives it its polite tone; but since it is still formally an imperative, people often switch to softer forms such as 「〜ていただけますか」 with superiors.
examples: Please open your textbooks to page 30.
Excuse me, please wait a moment.
Please take this medicine after meals.
Please speak a little more slowly.
Could you please write your name here?

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: A negative request, "please don't ...": 写真を撮らないでください (Please don't take photos). Attaches to the verb nai-form.

similar.title: 〜てくれる／〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜てくれませんか」 asks whether the other person is willing to do it, in question form; it is softer than 「〜てください」 and leaves room to refuse.

similar.title: 〜てもらう／〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Requests from the viewpoint of receiving a favor. 「〜ていただけませんか」 is the most common formal request and is more polite than 「〜てください」.

similar.title: Noun + をください
similar.explanation: 「水をください」 means "please give me (a thing)" and follows a noun; 「〜てください」 means "please do (an action)" and follows a verb te-form.

meaning: Please don't (do something). Used to politely forbid or discourage an action, or to tell someone they needn't do something.
connection: Verb nai-form + でください (e.g. 入る→入らないでください, 心配する→心配しないでください, 忘れる→忘れないでください)
usage: Made of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 + the conjunctive particle 「で」 + 「ください」. Note that it is 「ないで」, not 「なくて」: ×入らなくてください.
Forming the nai-form: godan verbs change the final sound to the a-row (書く→書かない); ichidan verbs drop る (見る→見ない); する→しない; 来る→こない; verbs ending in 「〜う」 become 「〜わない」 (買う→買わない).
Softer versions: 「〜ないでくださいませんか」, 「〜ないでいただけますか」; in casual speech among friends it is often shortened to 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ないでね」.
It sounds gentler than 「〜てはいけない」: 「〜てはいけない」 is a prohibition based on rules, while 「〜ないでください」 is the speaker's personal request.
Also often used out of consideration for the other person: 「気にしないでください」 (please don't worry about it), 「無理しないでください」 (please don't push yourself).
scenarios: Signs and announcements in public places: 「ここでタバコを吸わないでください。」
Notices in museums and galleries: 「作品に触らないでください。」
Comforting or showing concern for someone: 「心配しないでください。大丈夫ですから。」
Reminding someone not to forget: 「明日の約束、忘れないでくださいね。」
Between close people, 「ください」 is often dropped: 「行かないで」, 「泣かないで」.
etymology: 「ないで」 consists of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 and the conjunctive particle 「で」. It is generally thought that the negative auxiliary 「ない」 spread in the Kanto (Edo) dialect during the Edo period; before that, Classical Japanese 「ず」 was widely used, and "without doing ... and ..." was usually expressed as 「〜ずに」 or 「〜ずして」. 「ないで」 developed in Edo speech along with it. 「ください」 is the imperative of 「くださる（下さる）」 (see 〜てください). So 「〜ないでください」 literally means "please bestow on me the favor of not doing ...".
examples: Please don't smoke here.
Please don't touch the artwork.
Please don't worry. It's fine.
Please don't forget our plans for tomorrow, okay?

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: The affirmative request "please do ...", attached to the verb te-form: 座ってください (Please sit down).

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Expresses a prohibition based on rules or morals; stronger and more objective: ここで泳いではいけません (Swimming is not allowed here). 「〜ないでください」 is the speaker's request and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: "You don't have to": 来なくてもいいです (You don't need to come). Completely different from 「来ないでください」 (Please don't come).

meaning: 1) An action in progress (is ...ing); 2) a continuing state resulting from an action (has ... / is in a ... state); 3) habitual or repeated actions; 4) experience or record (something that happened in the past and stands as a present record).
connection: Verb te-form + いる (colloquial contraction: 〜てる／〜でる; humble or written: 〜ておる／〜ております)
usage: 「いる」 conjugates as an ichidan verb: ている／ています／ていた／ていない／ていません／ていて.

Durative verbs (読む, 食べる, 走る) + ている usually mean an action in progress: 本を読んでいる. Punctual (instantaneous) verbs (死ぬ, 結婚する, 来る, 知る) + ている express a resulting state: 結婚している (is married), 窓が開いている (the window is open).
For 「知る」, the affirmative is only 「知っている」, but the negative is 「知らない」 (not ×知っていない).
In speech the い is often dropped: 読んでる, 見てた, 知ってない; in Kansai and in humble written style, 「〜ておる／〜ております」 is used: お待ちしております.
Used to describe clothing, appearance, and states: 眼鏡をかけている (wears glasses), 赤い服を着ている (is wearing red clothes); and habits: 毎朝ジョギングしている.
scenarios: Describing what is happening right now: 「今、雨が降っています。」
Explaining a current state or status: 「兄は東京の会社に勤めています。」, 「もう結婚しています。」
Describing habits: 「毎朝6時に起きている。」
The humble form in business emails and announcements: 「皆様のお越しをお待ちしております。」
Casual contractions among friends: 「何してるの？」「テレビ見てる。」
etymology: 「いる」 was written 「ゐる」 (居る) in older Japanese and originally meant "to sit, to stay put somewhere". Classical Japanese used the auxiliaries 「たり」 and 「り」 to express the continuation or result of an action; from the medieval period on, 「〜てゐる」 (te-form + 居る) gradually developed and, in the modern era, became the main form for progressive and resultant states. Western Japan still widely uses 「〜とる／〜ておる」; 「おる」 (居る) was also originally a verb of existence, but in standard Japanese it became the humble or formal counterpart of 「いる」.
examples: It's raining right now.
My older brother works for a company in Tokyo.
The window is open, isn't it?
What are you doing? — I'm watching TV.
We look forward to welcoming you all.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: 「〜てある」 follows transitive verbs and emphasizes a state left behind after someone did something on purpose: 窓が開けてある (the window has been opened, deliberately); 「窓が開いている」 simply describes the window being open.

similar.title: 〜ているところだ
similar.explanation: Emphasizes "right in the middle of doing it at this moment": 今、ご飯を食べているところです. Highlights the point in time more than plain 「〜ている」.

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Expresses doing something in preparation for the future: ビールを冷やしておく; a different function from the state-describing 「〜ている」.

meaning: 1) Permission: may / can do ...; 2) in question form, asking permission: May I ...?; 3) 「〜なくてもいい」: don't have to ...; 4) concession or willingness: ... is fine too.
connection: Verb te-form + もいい; i-adjective 〜くて + もいい; na-adjective / noun + でもいい; negative: 〜なくてもいい
usage: 「いい」 can be replaced by 「よい／良い」 (written), 「かまわない／構わない」 (more formal), or 「大丈夫」 (casual): 写真を撮ってもかまいません.
Asking permission: 「〜てもいいですか」, 「〜てもよろしいですか」 (more polite); answers: 「ええ、どうぞ」, 「すみません、ちょっと…」.
「〜なくてもいい」 means "don't have to": 明日は来なくてもいいです (You don't need to come tomorrow).
With nouns / na-adjectives: 「明日でもいいですか」 (Is tomorrow okay?), 「安ければ、古くてもいい」 (If it's cheap, it's fine even if it's old).
The past tense of 「いい」 must be 「よかった」: 行ってもよかった (it would have been fine to go).
scenarios: Asking a teacher or shop staff for permission: 「この部屋で写真を撮ってもいいですか。」
A superior giving permission to a subordinate: 「今日はもう帰ってもいいですよ。」
Telling someone they don't need to do something: 「お金は今すぐ払わなくてもいいです。」
Conceding or offering to go along: 「手伝ってもいいよ。」 (I don't mind helping)
In formal situations: 「〜てもよろしいでしょうか」, 「〜ても構いませんか」.
etymology: Made of the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the concessive particle 「も」 ("even if") + the adjective 「いい」. Literally "even if you do ..., it is good", which extended to permission. 「いい」 is a colloquial variant of 「よい」; it is generally thought that forms such as 「えい」 and 「いい」 became popular in speech from the Edo period onward, while written language still mostly uses 「よい」. That is why its conjugations (よかった, よければ) are still based on 「よい」.
examples: May I take photos in this room?
You can go home now for today.
You don't have to pay right now.
Would it be all right if I sat here?
Is tomorrow okay?

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: The opposite of permission: prohibition. ここで写真を撮ってはいけません. Often used as the negative answer to 「〜てもいいですか」.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 「〜なくてもいい」 (don't have to) and 「〜なければならない」 (must) are opposites.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「〜ほうがいい」 is advice (you'd better ...); 「〜てもいい」 only grants permission (it's okay to ...) with no sense of recommendation.

meaning: Must not ..., not allowed to .... Expresses a prohibition based on rules or reason, or strongly discourages the listener.
connection: Verb te-form + はいけない (ては → colloquial 〜ちゃ; では → 〜じゃ); i-adjective 〜くては / noun・na-adjective 〜では + いけない
usage: Polite: 「〜てはいけません」; colloquial contractions: 「〜ちゃいけない」, 「〜じゃいけない」, 「〜ちゃだめ」.
「いけない」 can be replaced with 「だめだ」 (casual) or 「ならない」 (written, regulations, maxims): 嘘をついてはならない.
It is too blunt toward superiors; outside of explaining rules, people usually use 「〜ないでください」 or 「〜はご遠慮ください」 instead.
The negative question 「〜てはいけませんか」 asks for permission: 明日休んではいけませんか (Would it be all right if I took tomorrow off?).
Nouns / na-adjectives take 「では」: こんな字ではいけない (Handwriting like this won't do).
scenarios: School or company rules: 「授業中に携帯電話を使ってはいけません。」
Parents warning children: 「道路で遊んじゃだめ！」
Written language such as laws, notices, and maxims: 「人の物を盗んではならない。」
A doctor's instructions: 「今日はお風呂に入ってはいけません。」
etymology: 「いけない」 is the negative of the verb 「いける」 (行ける, "can go, works out"), originally meaning "cannot go, doesn't work", and by extension "no good, not allowed". 「〜ては」 = the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the topic particle 「は」, setting up a hypothetical condition: "if you do ..., it won't work", hence a prohibition. 「〜ちゃ」 and 「〜じゃ」 are contracted sound changes of 「ては」 and 「では」. In the written form 「〜てはならない」, 「ならない」 is the negative of 「成る」, meaning "won't hold, is not acceptable".
examples: You must not use your phone during class.
You can't swim here.
Don't play in the street!
One must not steal other people's things.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Asks the listener not to do something; softer, a personal request from the speaker: 写真を撮らないでください.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Expresses permission; the opposite of 「〜てはいけない」.

similar.title: 〜なければならない／〜なくてはいけない
similar.explanation: 「〜なくてはいけない」 (must) also contains 「てはいけない」, but it is preceded by the negative 「なく」, meaning "not doing it won't do" — the exact opposite of a prohibition.

meaning: Must ..., have to .... Expresses obligation or necessity (not doing it is not acceptable). Includes synonymous forms such as 〜なくてはいけない／〜なくちゃ／〜なきゃ／〜ないといけない.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + ければならない／くてはいけない; i-adjective 〜く + なければならない; noun・na-adjective + でなければならない
usage: The final part 「ならない」 and 「いけない」 are interchangeable: 〜なければいけない, 〜なくてはならない. Polite: 〜なければなりません／いけません.
「ならない」 is more formal and expresses social norms or objective obligations; 「いけない」 is more conversational and often expresses necessity in one's personal circumstances.
Colloquial contractions: なければ→なきゃ, なくては→なくちゃ, often with the second half omitted: 「もう行かなきゃ」, 「宿題しなくちゃ」.
「〜ないといけない／〜ないとだめ」 are also very common and more conversational.
For the negative (don't have to), use 「〜なくてもいい」; ×なければならなくない is not used.
scenarios: Explaining rules or obligations: 「日本では車は左側を走らなければなりません。」
Talking about your schedule or things you have to do: 「明日は早く起きなければならない。」
Taking leave among friends: 「あ、もうこんな時間。帰らなきゃ。」
Reminding yourself, talking to yourself: 「レポート、書かなくちゃ。」
Formal written or spoken expression such as papers and speeches: 「環境問題は世界全体で考えなければならない。」
etymology: 「なければ」 is the hypothetical form 「なけれ」 of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 + the conjunctive particle 「ば」 ("if not ..."), and 「ならない」 is the negative of the verb 「なる」 (成る, "to hold, to work out"). Literally, "if you don't do ..., it won't work" — a double negative expressing "must". 「なくては〜」 works the same way ("if you don't, then ..."). The colloquial 「なきゃ」 is a further contraction of 「なけりゃ」 (a sound change of なければ), and 「なくちゃ」 is a sound change of 「なくては」.
examples: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
Oh, it's already this late. I have to go home.
I've got to write my report.
You have to take the medicine every day.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Opposite: "don't have to": 今日は行かなくてもいい.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: Only advice (you'd better ...), without the obligation or compulsion of 「〜なければならない」.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Prohibition (must not). Note that 「〜なくてはいけない」 means "not doing it won't do" — the opposite of prohibition.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: An N2 written expression for "cannot help but", stressing that one is forced by circumstances to do something against one's will: 中止せざるを得ない.

meaning: 1) Proposes or calls on the listener to do something together with the speaker: Let's ...; 2) 「〜ましょうか」 offers to do something for the listener (Shall I ...?) or suggests doing something together (Shall we ...?); 3) used for instructions and calls to action (textbooks, notices).
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ましょう (e.g. 行きます→行きましょう, 休みます→休みましょう)
usage: It is the polite counterpart of 「〜よう／〜おう」 (volitional form): 行こう→行きましょう, 食べよう→食べましょう.
「〜ましょうか」 has two uses: (1) Shall we do it together? (行きましょうか); (2) offering help (荷物を持ちましょうか = Shall I carry your bags?).
When replying to an invitation, 「ええ、〜ましょう」 expresses agreement: 「行きませんか」「ええ、行きましょう」.
In notices, textbooks, and slogans it is a soft way of giving instructions: 「ゴミは持ち帰りましょう」, 「次の文を読みましょう」.
In casual speech it is sometimes said as 「〜ましょ」: さあ、行きましょ.
scenarios: Making a suggestion among coworkers or friends: 「そろそろ休みましょう。」
Offering to help someone: 「重そうですね。持ちましょうか。」
A teacher to students: 「では、教科書を読みましょう。」
Posters and notices: 「ゴミは決められた日に出しましょう。」
etymology: 「ましょう」 consists of 「ませ」, the irrealis form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」, and the conjectural/volitional auxiliary 「う」. 「う」 comes from Classical Japanese 「む」, which changed via 「ん」 to 「う」. 「ませう」 then became 「ましょう」 through palatalization. 「ます」 itself is generally thought to have evolved from 「まゐらす」 (参らす, a humble verb of offering) via 「まらする」 and 「まする」, becoming the ordinary polite auxiliary from the Edo period onward.
examples: Let's take a break soon.
That looks heavy. Shall I carry it for you?
Now then, let's read the textbook.
Please put out your garbage on the designated days.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: Invites the listener with a negative question, respecting their wishes; more polite than 「〜ましょう」. 「〜ましょう」 sounds more like a call to action, assuming you will do it together.

similar.title: 〜(よ)う
similar.explanation: The volitional form, the plain counterpart of 「〜ましょう」: 行こう！食べよう！ Used among friends.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: 「行こうと思う」 expresses the speaker's own plan, not a proposal to the listener.

meaning: Won't you ... (with me)? Why don't we ...? Politely invites or encourages the listener using a negative question.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ませんか (e.g. 行きます→行きませんか)
usage: By asking "won't you ...?" as a negative question, it leaves the decision to the listener; it respects their wishes more than 「〜ましょう」 and is the most common polite way to invite someone.
Often combined with 「一緒に」, 「よかったら」, 「今度」, etc.: よかったら、一緒に映画を見に行きませんか.
Accepting: 「いいですね、行きましょう」; declining: 「すみません、その日はちょっと…」 (indirect, without saying "no" outright).
Among friends, use the plain 「〜ない？」: 一緒に帰らない？ (rising intonation).
Note: 「わかりませんか」, 「ありませんか」, etc. are ordinary negative questions (Don't you understand? / Isn't there any?), not invitations; 「〜てくれませんか」 and 「〜てくださいませんか」 are requests.
scenarios: Inviting coworkers or friends: 「週末、一緒にテニスをしませんか。」
Offering someone something: 「お茶でも飲みませんか。」
Making a suggestion: 「ちょっと休みませんか。」
Inviting someone you've just met; more polite than 「〜ましょう」.
etymology: 「ません」 is 「ませ」, the irrealis form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」, plus the negative auxiliary 「ぬ」 (which changed to 「ん」). The final 「か」 is the question particle. Inviting through a negative question is a common indirect strategy in Japanese: instead of saying "let's go", you ask "won't you go?", leaving the other person room to say no.
examples: Would you like to play tennis together this weekend?
How about some tea?
If you'd like, why don't you come over to my place sometime?
Shall we take a short break?

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: 「〜ましょう」 means "let's ..."; it is more assertive and assumes the listener will agree. 「〜ませんか」 first asks for the listener's wishes and is more polite.

similar.title: 〜ましょうか
similar.explanation: Suggests doing something together (行きましょうか) or offers help (手伝いましょうか).

similar.title: 〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: Asks the listener to do something for you (a request), not an invitation to do it together.

meaning: 1) Gives a few representative examples out of several actions: things like ... and ...; 2) two opposite actions alternating: sometimes ..., sometimes ...; 3) a single 「〜たりする」 softly gives one example: ... or something like that.
connection: Verb ta-form + り (だり when the ta-form ends in だ), 〜たり〜たりする; i-adjective 〜かったり; noun・na-adjective 〜だったり
usage: The pattern usually ends with 「する」, which carries tense and politeness: 「〜たり〜たりしました」. 「〜たり〜たりです」 is mostly used in noun-like descriptions (毎日、洗濯したり掃除したりです).
The list is non-exhaustive and implies "among other things"; to list actions in sequence, use 「〜て、〜て」.
Alternating opposite actions: 行ったり来たりする (go back and forth), 泣いたり笑ったり (crying and laughing by turns).
With adjectives and nouns, it expresses an unstable state: 天気は晴れたり曇ったり, 値段は高かったり安かったり.
A single 「〜たりする」 gives a soft example or expresses uncertainty: たまに一人で映画を見たりします.
scenarios: Describing weekend or holiday activities: 「休みの日は本を読んだり、音楽を聞いたりします。」
Describing back-and-forth movement: 「彼は部屋の中を行ったり来たりしている。」
Saying conditions keep changing: 「最近は暑かったり寒かったりで、体調を崩しやすい。」
A gentle warning: 「授業中に寝たりしないでください。」
etymology: 「たり」 comes from the Classical Japanese perfective/continuative auxiliary 「たり」, which is itself a contraction of 「て」 + 「あり」 (てあり→たり). From the medieval period on, 「〜たり〜たり」 was used to list two or more actions, gradually developing into the modern listing use. The modern past auxiliary 「た」 also arose from 「たる」, the attributive form of 「たり」, losing its final syllable; so 「たり」 and 「た」 share the same origin, and both show the same voicing in 「〜んだり」 and 「〜いだり」.
examples: On my days off, I do things like read books and listen to music.
He is pacing back and forth in the room.
Lately it's been hot one day and cold the next.
Please don't do things like sleeping in class.

similar.title: 〜て、〜て
similar.explanation: Connects actions in chronological order and lists all of them: 朝起きて、顔を洗って、ご飯を食べます. 「〜たり」 only gives examples, with no order.

similar.title: 〜し、〜し
similar.explanation: Lists reasons or features (... and what's more ...), mostly to explain causes: 安いし、おいしいし、よく行く.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Two actions happening at the same time: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する; 「〜たり〜たり」 means doing them alternately or separately.

meaning: Have (ever) done .... Expresses past experience; the negative 「〜たことがない」 means "have never done ...".
connection: Verb ta-form + ことがある (negative: 〜たことがない; polite: 〜たことがあります／ありません)
usage: Expresses life experience, usually something not done often and worth mentioning. It is not used for recent everyday actions like "went to the supermarket yesterday"; just say 「昨日スーパーへ行きました」.
Question: 「〜たことがありますか」; answers: 「はい、あります」, 「いいえ、ありません／一度もありません」.
In speech 「が」 is often dropped or replaced with 「は／も」: 食べたことある？, 行ったことはない, 見たこともない.
Often combined with 「一度」, 「何度も」, 「まだ」, or 「一度も〜ない」: 富士山には一度も登ったことがない.
Don't confuse it with "dictionary form + ことがある" (sometimes ...): たまに遅刻することがある (I'm occasionally late), which has nothing to do with experience.
scenarios: Talking about experiences when first meeting someone: 「日本へ行ったことがありますか。」
Talking about foods you've eaten: 「納豆は食べたことがありません。」
Emphasizing something rare: 「こんなきれいな景色は見たことがない。」
Describing your experience in an interview or self-introduction: 「中国で働いたことがあります。」
etymology: Made of the past auxiliary 「た」 + the formal noun 「こと」 (事, "matter, fact") + the case particle 「が」 + the existential verb 「ある」. Literally "there exists the fact of having done ...", i.e. "to have the experience of ...". 「た」 comes from the classical perfective auxiliary 「たり」 (て + あり). 「こと」 is written with the kanji 「事」, but as a grammatical formal noun it is usually written in kana.
examples: Have you ever been to Japan?
I've never eaten natto, not even once.
I've never seen such beautiful scenery.
Have you read that book?

similar.title: Dictionary form + ことがある
similar.explanation: Means "sometimes ...": 日曜日でも会社へ行くことがある. Follows the dictionary form and has nothing to do with experience.

similar.title: 〜ことにする／〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Also use 「こと」, but express decisions (deciding oneself / being decided), not experience.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Means "have just ...", stressing that it happened very recently; 「〜たことがある」 only says whether you have the experience, regardless of when.

meaning: Before .... Indicates that the action in the main clause happens before the action (or event) in the preceding clause.
connection: Verb dictionary form + まえに; noun + の + まえに; time-quantity expression + まえに (三年前に = three years ago)
usage: The preceding verb is always in the dictionary form, even if the whole sentence is in the past: ×寝た前に → ○寝る前に歯を磨いた.
It can be followed by 「に」 to mark a point in time, and other particles such as 「前は」, 「前から」, or 「前で」 are possible, but 「前に」 is the most common for "do something before ...".
For time, "noun + の + 前に" usually takes action nouns (食事, 試験, 出発, 授業); 「駅の前に」 is a location ("in front of the station"), not this grammar point.
Quantity expressions attach directly to 「前に」: 三年前に日本に来ました (I came to Japan three years ago).
Usually written with the kanji 「前に」; children's books and textbooks sometimes write 「まえに」 in kana.
scenarios: Describing daily habits: 「寝る前に歯を磨きます。」
Reminders and instructions: 「出かける前に、窓を閉めてください。」
Arranging the order of things: 「授業の前に宿題を出しなさい。」
Explaining rules: 「食事の前に手を洗いましょう。」
etymology: 「まえ」 is written 「前」. Its origin is generally thought to be 「ま（目）」 (eye) + 「へ（方）」 (direction), i.e. "the direction the eyes face", originally meaning "in front" in space. It later extended from a spatial to a temporal meaning ("ahead of a certain moment"), giving the temporal use of 「〜前に」. This shift from space to time is common across languages; English "before" likewise originally meant "in front of" (as in "stand before the king").
examples: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Please close the windows before you go out.
Let's wash our hands before eating.
Before coming to Japan, I studied a little Japanese.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: Opposite: "after ...", preceded by the verb ta-form: ご飯を食べた後で、散歩します.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: Means "while (the state hasn't changed yet)": 暗くならないうちに帰ろう. It stresses seizing the opportunity, whereas 「前に」 is only about time order.

similar.title: 〜までに
similar.explanation: Expresses a deadline, "by ...": 5時までに来てください; 「前に」 only states order and doesn't stress a deadline.

meaning: After .... Indicates that the action in the main clause happens after the preceding action is completed.
connection: Verb ta-form + あとで (後で); noun + の + あとで
usage: The preceding verb is always in the ta-form, even when the sentence refers to the future: ご飯を食べた後で、散歩します.
「で」 can be dropped: 「〜た後、〜」 (common in writing and news); 「〜た後に」 emphasizes the point in time; 「〜た後は」 contrasts before and after.
Noun form: 授業の後で, 仕事の後で.
「あとで」 used on its own is an adverb meaning "later, afterwards": あとで電話します.
Compared with 「〜てから」, 「〜た後で」 simply states the order; there can be a long gap between the two actions, and it doesn't stress "immediately after".
scenarios: Describing a daily routine: 「仕事が終わった後で、ジムに行きます。」
Explaining precautions: 「食べた後で、すぐに運動しないでください。」
Narrating past events: 「映画を見た後、レストランで食事をした。」
Scheduling: 「会議の後で、少し話しましょう。」
etymology: 「あと」 is written 「後」 or 「跡」, originally meaning "footprint, trace"; it is generally considered cognate with 「跡」 (one theory derives it from 「あ（足）」 "foot" + 「と（処）」 "place"). From "the trace left after passing" it came to mean "behind" in space, and then "after" in time. 「で」 is a case particle marking a time frame or circumstance. 「〜た後で」 literally means "in the time after having done ...".
examples: After work, I go to the gym.
After watching the movie, we ate at a restaurant.
You can play games after you've done your homework.
Let's talk a bit after the meeting.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: Emphasizes "do the next thing only after finishing the first", with the actions closely linked, often expressing a necessary order: 手を洗ってから食べなさい. 「〜た後で」 is just simple time order.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Opposite: before ..., preceded by the dictionary form: 寝る前に.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: "Have just done", stressing that very little time has passed: 今ご飯を食べたばかりです.

meaning: 1) While ...ing: the same subject does two actions at the same time; 2) (advanced) although ...: expresses contrast (N2 level, e.g. 「知りながら」, 「残念ながら」).
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ながら (e.g. 聞きます→聞きながら, 食べます→食べながら)
usage: Both actions must have the same subject. The main action goes at the end of the sentence; the action before 「ながら」 is the secondary, accompanying one: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する (the main activity is studying).
The preceding verb is generally durative (聞く, 歩く, 食べる); punctual verbs (着く, 死ぬ) cannot be used for "while doing".
It can also express long-term parallel activities: 働きながら大学に通う (attend university while working).
「ながら」 can be followed by 「も」: 「〜ながらも」 expresses contrast, "although ..., still ..." — a more advanced use.
Set phrases: 「残念ながら」 (unfortunately), 「昔ながらの」 (traditional, as in the old days), 「涙ながらに」 (in tears).
scenarios: Describing daily habits: 「コーヒーを飲みながら新聞を読みます。」
Safety warnings: 「歩きながらスマホを見ないでください。」
Describing one's lifestyle: 「アルバイトをしながら日本語学校に通っています。」
Contrast in written language: 「悪いと知りながら、嘘をついてしまった。」
etymology: 「ながら」 already existed in Classical Japanese. It is generally thought to come from the Old Japanese genitive particle 「な」 (equivalent to 「の」) + the noun 「から」 ("nature, original state, same condition", cognate with 「柄（がら）」), originally meaning "keeping the original state of ...", as in 「昔ながら」 (just as in the old days) and 「涙ながら」 (with tears). From "maintaining a state" it developed both the meaning "while an action continues" (simultaneity) and the contrastive meaning "although in a certain state, ...".
examples: I read the newspaper while drinking coffee.
Please don't look at your phone while walking.
I attend a Japanese language school while working part-time.
My mother is cooking while singing.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Lists actions or describes them alternating, not necessarily at the same time: 歌ったり踊ったりする.

similar.title: 〜つつ
similar.explanation: Written language, similar to 「ながら」, with both "simultaneous" and "contrastive" meanings: 体に悪いと知りつつ、タバコをやめられない.

similar.title: 〜ているあいだ（に）
similar.explanation: "During ..."; the subjects of the two clauses can differ: 母が料理をしている間、私は掃除をした. 「ながら」 requires the same subject.

meaning: Because ..., so .... Expresses a cause or reason; relatively subjective, often used to give grounds for the speaker's judgment, intention, request, or command.
connection: Plain or polite form of verbs / i-adjectives + から; noun・na-adjective + だから／ですから
usage: It can follow the plain or polite form: 雨が降るから／雨が降りますから; nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: 雨だから, 静かだから.
The main clause can be a command, request, intention, guess, or other subjective expression: 危ないから、触らないで. In this respect it is freer than 「ので」.
It can stand at the end of a sentence as 「〜からだ／〜からです」 to state the reason: 遅れたのは、電車が止まったからです.
When answering 「どうして」, you can give just the reason: 「どうして休んだの？」「熱があったから。」
Distinguish it from the case particle 「から」 marking a starting point (東京から, 9時から); 「〜てから」 means "after doing ..." and is not a reason either.
scenarios: Giving a reason with a request: 「時間がないから、急いでください。」
Explaining among friends: 「今日は疲れたから、早く寝るね。」
Answering why: 「どうして遅れたんですか。」「バスが来なかったからです。」
Warnings: 「危ないから、触らないで！」
etymology: 「から」 was originally a case particle marking a starting point or route ("from ..."). As for its origin, it is generally thought to be cognate with the noun 「柄（から）」 (nature, cause, root), though there are other theories. Since a cause can be seen as the "starting point" of an event, the starting-point 「から」 naturally extended to a conjunctive particle of cause and reason; this use became widespread from the medieval period onward. (Compare English "from" in "suffering from the cold".)
examples: We're out of time, so please hurry.
I'm tired today, so I'm going to bed early.
Tomorrow is a day off, so please take it easy.
The reason I was late is that the train stopped.
It's raining, so I don't want to go out.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: 「ので」 is more objective and polite, often used to explain reasons or apologize to superiors; 「から」 is more subjective and sounds more natural before commands or intentions. For example, when asking for a day off, 「熱があるので、休ませてください」 is more appropriate than using 「から」.

similar.title: 〜おかげで／〜せいで
similar.explanation: Both express a cause but with emotional coloring: 「おかげで」 is for good results (gratitude), 「せいで」 for bad results (blame).

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: "It's all because of ...", blaming a cause for a bad result: 雨のせいで試合が中止になった.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: "After doing ...", expressing time order, not a reason: ご飯を食べてから出かける.

meaning: Because ..., (so) .... Expresses a cause or reason in a more objective, softer, and more polite tone than 「から」; mostly used to state objective cause-and-effect or to explain a situation.
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + ので; noun・na-adjective + なので (e.g. 雨なので, 静かなので); in formal speech the polite form + ので is also possible (〜ますので, 〜ですので)
usage: Nouns and na-adjectives take 「なので」, not 「だので」: 学生なので, 暇なので.
「ので」 presents the cause-and-effect as an objective fact, so it suits explaining reasons, apologizing, or asking permission from superiors and clients: 体調が悪いので、早退させていただけますか.
In formal situations you can say 「〜ますので」 or 「〜ですので」: 資料をお送りしますので、ご確認ください.
In casual speech it is often pronounced 「んで」: 時間ないんで、また今度.
It is generally not used at the end of a sentence as 「〜のでだ」; to put a reason at the end, use 「〜からだ」. Note that 「〜のです／〜のではない」 is the explanatory 「のだ」, not 「ので」.
scenarios: Explaining the reason when asking for leave or apologizing: 「熱があるので、今日は休ませてください。」
Business emails: 「来週出張しますので、返信が遅れるかもしれません。」
Objectively explaining a situation: 「この道は狭いので、車が通れません。」
Shop notices: 「本日は定休日なので、お休みです。」
etymology: 「ので」 combines the nominalizing particle (formal noun) 「の」 with 「で」, the continuative form of the copula 「だ」; literally something like "it is the fact that ..., (so)". It is generally thought that this form began to be used as a conjunctive particle in the late Edo period and became widespread after the Meiji era. Because it explains a cause by nominalizing the preceding clause (「の」) and then asserting it, it feels more objective and softer than 「から」.
examples: I have a fever, so please let me take today off.
This road is narrow, so cars can't get through.
Tomorrow is Sunday, so there's no school.
I'll send you the materials, so please take a look.

similar.title: 〜から
similar.explanation: More subjective; can be followed by commands, intentions, or guesses. 「ので」 is more objective and polite. 「危ないから触るな」 sounds natural, but with 「ので」 it would sound awkward.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Also attaches via 「の」, but expresses contrast, "even though ...", with dissatisfaction or surprise: 雨なのに、傘を持っていない.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Written language, expressing cause (台風のために) or purpose (留学するために); more formal than 「ので」.

meaning: Want (something). Expresses the speaker's desire for a thing; in questions, asks what the listener wants.
connection: Noun + が + ほしい (欲しい); ほしい conjugates as an i-adjective
usage: 「ほしい」 is an i-adjective: ほしい／ほしくない／ほしかった／ほしくて; for politeness add 「です」: ほしいです.
The desired object is marked with 「が」 (not ×を ほしい); in negatives or contrasts it often becomes 「は」: 車はほしくない.
In principle it is used only for the first person and the second person in questions; for a third person use 「ほしがる／ほしがっている」: 弟は新しいゲームをほしがっている.
Asking a superior directly 「何がほしいですか」 is not very polite; you can say 「何かご希望はありますか」 instead.
「〜てほしい」 (wanting someone else to do something) is a different use: 早く元気になってほしい.
scenarios: Saying what you want: 「新しいパソコンがほしいです。」
Asking a friend: 「誕生日に何がほしい？」
Saying you don't need anything: 「今は何もほしくない。」
Recalling a past wish: 「子どものころ、犬がほしかった。」
etymology: 「ほしい」 comes from the Classical Japanese adjective 「ほし」 (欲し, shiku-type conjugation), cognate with the old verb 「ほる」 (欲る, "to want"). The attributive form 「ほしき」 became 「ほしい」 through i-onbin. It is written 「欲しい」 in kanji, but as an auxiliary adjective (〜てほしい) it is usually written in kana.
examples: I want a new computer.
What do you want for your birthday?
I don't want anything right now.
When I was a child, I really wanted a dog.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: Wanting to do an action; follows the verb masu-stem: 車を買いたい. 「ほしい」 follows a noun and means wanting the thing itself.

similar.title: 〜てほしい
similar.explanation: Wanting someone else (not yourself) to do something: もっとゆっくり話してほしい.

similar.title: 〜ほしがる
similar.explanation: Used for a third person: 子どもがおもちゃをほしがっている.

meaning: 1) Intend to, plan to ... (an intention or plan thought out in advance); 2) 「ta-form / noun の + つもり」: believe (mistakenly) that ..., consider it as ... (a perception that doesn't match reality).
connection: Verb dictionary form + つもりだ; negative: verb nai-form + つもりだ (intend not to) / dictionary form + つもりはない (have no intention at all); verb ta-form・noun の + つもり
usage: Expresses a considered, fairly firm intention; more planned than 「〜たい」 (a wish) or 「〜(よ)うと思う」 (a thought one has at the moment).
There are two negatives: 「行かないつもりだ」 (I intend not to go) and 「行くつもりはない」 (I have no intention whatsoever of going; stronger).
Asking a superior directly 「〜つもりですか」 can sound like interrogating their intentions and is not very polite; say 「〜ご予定ですか」 instead.
「〜たつもり」: thinking you have done something when you actually haven't: 鍵をかけたつもりだったが、開いていた.
「Noun のつもり」: treating it as ...: 旅行のつもりで出張を楽しむ; 「どういうつもりだ」 (What do you think you're doing?) is an accusation.
scenarios: Talking about plans: 「来年、日本に留学するつもりです。」
Expressing a resolution not to do something: 「もう二度とタバコは吸わないつもりだ。」
Making your position clear when declining: 「その会社に入るつもりはありません。」
Justifying yourself or reflecting: 「冗談のつもりだったんです。」
etymology: 「つもり」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「積もる」 (つもる, "to pile up", extended to "to estimate, to calculate"). Written 「積もり」 or 「積り」, it originally meant "estimate, budget", a sense still preserved in 「見積もり」 (quotation, estimate). From "estimating in advance" it came to mean "one's inner calculation, intention". 「心算」 is a borrowed-kanji spelling for this meaning; today it is generally written in kana as 「つもり」.
examples: I plan to study abroad in Japan next year.
I'm determined never to smoke again.
I have no intention of joining that company.
I thought I had locked it, but it was open.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Expresses an intention that occurs to the speaker at the moment; less resolute than 「つもり」: 週末は映画を見ようと思う.

similar.title: 〜予定だ
similar.explanation: Expresses a fixed schedule, often an objective plan involving others: 会議は3時から始まる予定です.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: Expresses having made a decision: 来年留学することにした. 「つもり」 is an inner intention; 「ことにする」 stresses the act of deciding.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: Only a wish, not necessarily backed by a plan to act.

meaning: You'd better ..., it would be best to .... Gives advice or a warning to the listener; the negative 「〜ないほうがいい」 means "you'd better not ...".
connection: Verb ta-form + ほうがいい (advise doing); verb nai-form + ほうがいい (advise not doing); the dictionary form is also possible
usage: When advising someone to do something, the ta-form is generally used: 早く寝たほうがいい. The dictionary form (早く寝るほうがいい) leans toward general statements or comparisons.
To advise against something, use 「〜ないほうがいい」; ×〜なかったほうがいい is not used.
「いい」 can be replaced with 「よい／良い」 (written) or 「よろしい」 (formal). Polite: 〜たほうがいいですよ.
The tone is fairly direct; saying 「〜たほうがいいです」 to a superior can sound like you're lecturing them, so the softer 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 is better.
The past 「〜たほうがよかった」 expresses regret: もっと勉強したほうがよかった (I should have studied more).
scenarios: Showing concern or advising a friend: 「顔色が悪いよ。今日は早く寝たほうがいい。」
Advice from a doctor or senior: 「タバコはやめたほうがいいですよ。」
Warning against something: 「夜、一人で歩かないほうがいい。」
Reflecting on the past: 「もっと早く出発したほうがよかった。」
etymology: 「ほう」 is written 「方」, originally meaning "direction, side", and by extension "one side" of two alternatives. 「〜ほうがいい」 literally means "the side of (doing ...) is better". It was originally a comparative expression (AよりBのほうがいい); the item being compared was later omitted, and it became a fixed pattern for giving advice. 「いい」 is the colloquial form of 「よい」, so its past tense is 「よかった」.
examples: You look pale. You'd better go to bed early today.
You really should quit smoking.
You'd better not walk alone at night.
We should have left earlier.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Expresses obligation (must); far more compelling than 「ほうがいい」.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Expresses permission (it's okay to); no sense of recommendation.

similar.title: Noun + のほうがいい
similar.explanation: Compares preferences between two things: コーヒーより紅茶のほうがいい (I'd prefer tea to coffee); not advice.

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: Also gives advice, but more softly, like offering an option: 病院に行ったらどうですか.
